To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the mental health and educational attainment of children and families living in poverty is impacted by a range of risk and resilience factors, and that the problem cannot be solved by schools alone.

the impact of social stratifications, poverty and adverse childhood experiences on the mental health, wellbeing and attainment of Scottish children and young people can be understood and addressed through the lens of the resilience framework.
the mental health and attainment of children is impacted by the interplay of risk factors, protective factors, mediating variables and policy.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the inter-relationships between poverty, mental health and wellbeing, and attainment, and the impact of these on resilience.
the impact of poverty on children’s mental health, wellbeing and attainment, and with how this impact can be reduced.
the impact of social inequalities and poverty on the attainment, mental health and wellbeing of children and young in Scotland.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the mental health and educational attainment of children and their families living in poverty is a problem in Scotland, which is a consequence of a range of factors, including social stratification.
the problem cannot be addressed without taking a holistic approach to the problem and that the problem is a societal one.

there is a strong and growing body of research which suggests a causal link between poverty and poor mental health and wellbeing, and that there is a causal link between poor mental health and low attainment.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we need to develop and sustain a ‘whole child’ approach that recognises the inter-relationship between children’s mental health, wellbeing and attainment, and to do this in the context of a supportive community.
the findings support the view that the problem is complex and multi-faceted, but that it can be tackled and that the solution lies in the hands of the Scottish Government and its agencies.

the findings support the need to develop a more holistic, integrated approach to addressing the impact of social stratifications and adverse childhood experiences on the mental health, wellbeing and attainment of young people living in poverty.
The main takeaway from our work is that

there is a strong need to develop a holistic approach to the problem that takes account of the inter-relationships of the various factors impacting on children’s attainment, mental health and wellbeing.
we need to be ambitious in tackling poverty-related inequality in the lives of children and young adults, and to recognise that this is not simply an educational problem.
there is a strong need for a whole system, whole school and whole family approach to addressing the problem.
